question.text: From FY 2024-25, which tax regime is the default for individual taxpayers?

answer.text: Old tax regime with all deductions available
The taxpayer must mandatorily choose a regime every year; there is no default
New tax regime is the default; the taxpayer must actively opt out to choose the old regime
Old regime for salaried individuals and new regime for business income earners

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the amended Section 115BAC framework, the new tax regime (with concessional slab rates and limited deductions) is the default regime for individual taxpayers from FY 2024-25 onwards. A taxpayer who wishes to be taxed under the old regime (with traditional deductions and exemptions) must affirmatively opt out, typically by filing Form 10-IEA within the prescribed timelines. If no opt-out is exercised, the return is processed under the new regime by default. The Trap: "Old tax regime with all deductions available" reflects the pre-amendment position when the old regime was default. "Must mandatorily choose a regime every year; there is no default" denies the existence of a default at all, which is incorrect after the amendment. "Old regime for salaried individuals and new regime for business income earners" invents a category-based split that is not how the default rule is framed — the default applies uniformly to individuals. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages set out the Section 115BAC slab rates and rebate rules but do not explicitly state that the new regime is the default from FY 2024-25 or that taxpayers must opt out via Form 10-IEA. The default-regime and Form 10-IEA framing above is presented as general direct-tax regulatory knowledge, not as a workbook-page citation.
